summary: An excerpt from Kate Douglas Wiggin's novel Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, in which Rebecca comforts her bedridden mother Aurelia, who laments that their hopes for Rebecca's education and future have been wasted. Rebecca answers cheerfully, comparing her youth to a tree's slow growing season and playfully claiming to be a princess in disguise awaiting her kingdom. Aurelia is partly comforted but worries about the family's hardships, including Miranda's disability, and Rebecca's responsibilities at the farm.
one_line: Rebecca cheers her bedridden mother Aurelia, who despairs over lost hopes, with talk of growing season and a secret princess kingdom.
key_facts: Aurelia cries that she is chained to the bed and that her saving, Rebecca's hard study, and Mirandy's outlay have all been wasted.
Rebecca is only a little past seventeen years old, per her own words in this passage.
Rebecca compares herself to a young tree that did not grow during a dry summer and cold winter but caught up in a good year.
Rebecca calls her current period her 'rooting season' and says her day has not yet begun.
Rebecca notes that the old maple by the well, in its hundredth year, had new leaves that summer, giving her hope at seventeen.
Aurelia says Rebecca has lost her place and will never see her friends there, calling her a drudge.
Rebecca jokingly claims she is a princess in disguise whose king and queen are very old and about to abdicate in her favor.
Rebecca describes her future kingdom as small, with an ivory throne and a screen of peacock feathers rather than a golden throne.
Aurelia smiles in spite of herself and is comforted, though not wholly deceived.
Aurelia says life looks hard to her because Miranda is a cripple at the brick house and she is another invalid at the farm.
Aurelia names Jenny, Fanny and Mark as further burdens tying Rebecca hand and foot.
Aurelia observes that Rebecca has something of her father's happy disposition.
Rebecca says it is enough joy just to be alive in the world on a day like this.
